summary:
Antioquia stands under Colombia's national framework, which since a rule change approved in June 2015 has allowed the sex marker on government-issued identification to be changed by signing a document before a notary. That replaced the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, with no surgical requirement. Marriage has been available to same-sex couples since 2016 and adoption since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Detention sits inside the same protection framework. A Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, upholding the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that rising killings demand urgent attention.

Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent case. In Bello, near Medellín, Sara Millerey González Borja, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight in early April 2025 while onlookers filmed her. The footage went viral on 5 April. She died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello that year, after two gay men, and one report counted 13 trans people killed across Colombia in the first quarter of 2025.

Official response came quickly but the case also exposed institutional failure. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, solidarity events and protests were held in several cities, and Bello's city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name. A clinic reportedly declined to treat her as an emergency "because she didn't get shot". Her mother, Sandra Borja, said, "They killed her for being who she was".
tangentialFactors:
The clearest escalation elsewhere in Colombia is territorially announced violence by armed groups. In Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, armed groups distributed flyers on streets and through WhatsApp announcing a "social cleansing" plan naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets; trans women in the department fled after death threats, and one trans salon owner, Tatiana Cespedes, relocated twice after armed men threatened her, while a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In Guajira, flyers posted from March 2024 carried a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

The Antioquia case belongs to a different setting: ordinary urban violence rather than an announced campaign, which is the pattern recorded in the national tallies. Forty-one transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023, eight more between February and April 2024, and 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025; the Attorney General's Office counted 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against them constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on their identification by signing a document before a notary; since 2015 no judge, bodily inspection or psychiatric assessment is required, and Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-recognition without surgery. Same-sex couples have been able to marry since 2016 and adopt since 2015, and identity documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

A comprehensive trans law remained before the legislature during 2025, so the protections in force rest on notary procedure, constitutional jurisprudence and court rulings rather than a single consolidated statute.

Institutional conduct toward trans residents remains a live issue. Bello's city hall was criticised for using Sara Millerey González Borja's pre-transition name after her killing, and a clinic reportedly refused to treat her as an emergency on the ground that she had not been shot. vigils, protests and solidarity events followed in several cities, and the President ordered an investigation.

Trans people deprived of liberty have judicial protection: a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman in custody and on the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this record establishes what protection machinery the Antioquia departmental government or the Medellín and Bello municipal authorities maintain specifically for trans people, such as a protection unit, police protocol or hate-crime charging practice. That remains unresolved.

The sources date the viral footage to 5 April 2025 and her death to cardiac arrest the following afternoon; the exact date of the assault itself is not fixed in the material available here.

Whether the clinic's refusal to treat her was investigated, and whether the comprehensive trans law under consideration in 2025 has since been enacted, are not sourced in this inventory.

The national kill tallies for 2023, 2024 and the first quarter of 2025 are not broken down by department, so Antioquia's share of those figures cannot be stated from these sources.

Flyer-based "social cleansing" and kill-list campaigns are documented for Caquetá and Guajira. No source in this record confirms equivalent announced campaigns inside Antioquia, and armed-group presence levels within the department are not covered here.
